title: Terrain Elevation Grid Map: Slopes Cell by Cell
description: Map slopes cell by cell from a 9×9 elevation sample with the Terrain Elevation Grid Map — see where the ground tilts, and how hard. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, around a point on a Colorado foothill the grid can read gentle 4% cells on the bench and 38% cells in the gully two cells over — the slope pattern a single centre elevation could never tell you.
quick_answer: The Terrain Elevation Grid Map samples elevations on a 9×9 grid around your point and turns them into a cell-by-cell slope map, each cell coloured by its steepest gradient in percent. Set the centre and area size and read the pattern — benches, gullies and scarps made visible.

The same hillside sampled with a small area gives small cells and sharp detail; a large area averages slopes down. A 30% gully wall inside a gentle cell reads as that cell's maximum gradient — pattern first, precision by zooming in.
A straight line of steep cells crossing otherwise calm ground is a scarp, terrace edge or road cut — linear features announce themselves in grids long before they are named.

popular_table.note: Slopes come from sampled elevations (Open-Meteo elevation data over the grid), so a feature narrower than a cell can be softened or missed. It is a scouting lens, not a survey.

faq: Detail follows the area you choose: the 9×9 grid divides your selected area, so small areas give metre-scale cells and large areas give broad-brush cells. The elevation source itself resolves features down to roughly 90 m in its underlying model.
Why the maximum gradient per cell?
Water, wheels and feet all care about the steepest direction, not the average. Each cell reports its steepest downhill gradient so hazards are not averaged away.
Can I get one exact slope instead?
Yes — pick the two elevations yourself and use the Slope & Gradient Calculator for a single precise figure. This map is for pattern; that tool is for a number.
What elevation data does it use?
Open-Meteo's elevation sampling, built on global terrain models (Copernicus-class data). The atlas sibling samples a 7×7 grid of raw elevations from the same source family.
Does vegetation or buildings affect it?
Terrain models aim for bare earth, but processing varies; dense forest canopy and dense urban areas can bias sampled heights in the source data.
Water surfaces read at their surface elevation with near-zero slope — flat blue honesty at the grid's edge.
The grid is computed in your browser for viewing. For GIS work, the same public elevation sources can be loaded directly into QGIS or similar tools.
